solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Greed a weakness, tart essentially scoffed (7)

indicatorNotes.essentially: the essence of a word is its core, so take the middle letters
indicatorNotes.scoffed: to scoff is to eat, so one piece swallows the other

blocks.note: a vice is a moral weakness
the middle two letters of tART

annotation.surface: Someone confesses that their greed made them wolf down a tart.
annotation.walkthrough: The picture of scoffing a tart hides that the eater is the weakness and the thing eaten is only the tart's middle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: avarice is the specific greed for money and possessions, one of the seven deadly sins.

entries.clue: Trees in centre of Seattle, initially (2,5)

indicatorNotes.in: the trees sit inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.centre of: take the middle of the word

blocks.note: the middle three letters of seATTle

annotation.surface: A note about trees growing in the heart of Seattle.
annotation.walkthrough: Seattle has seven letters, so its centre is taken as the middle three rather than a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both phrases mark the opening stage of something before it changed.

entries.clue: Everywhere at sea? (3,4,3,5)

annotation.surface: Wondering whether being everywhere means being out on the ocean.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At sea' reads as on the ocean, but here it is the idiom for bewildered, which is the second sense of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses hold: literally spread across every place, and idiomatically disorganised or confused.

entries.clue: Hearts in bid strong, also one club (4)

indicatorNotes.Hearts in: the heart of a word is its middle, so take the middles of the words that follow

blocks.note: the middle two letters of stROng

annotation.surface: A bridge player bids strongly in hearts and also shows one club.
annotation.walkthrough: Hearts and club look like card suits from a bridge auction; hearts means middles and the club is a golf club.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: golfers carry several irons, metal-headed clubs, alongside woods and a putter.

entries.clue: Drain pipe (7)

blocks.note: as a verb: to use up completely
the tube carrying fumes away from a car's engine

annotation.surface: Plumbing: a drainpipe.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words read together as 'drainpipe'; split them and one is a verb, the other a car part.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb, to use something up entirely, and the noun, the tailpipe expelling engine gases.

entries.clue: Stream of income easily milked? (4,3)

blocks.note: the surface reads as a flow of money from a business
read literally: an animal that gives milk readily

annotation.surface: A business source of money that can be exploited without effort.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Milked' is the cryptic touch: a business that can be milked is pictured as a literal dairy animal that yields money.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from business: a product that keeps yielding profit for little investment, like a cow giving milk.

entries.clue: Topical fruit, did you say? (7)

indicatorNotes.did you say?: asks whether we heard it right, so the answer sounds like the fruit

blocks.note: a currant is a small dried fruit

annotation.surface: Someone asks if a fashionable fruit was mentioned.
annotation.walkthrough: The dried fruit and the answer are pronounced the same but spelt differently.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something current belongs to the present, as topical news does.

entries.clue: Spot something hideous in audition? (4)

indicatorNotes.in audition: audition is hearing, so the answer is what the phrase sounds like

annotation.surface: A talent-show judge spots an ugly act at an audition.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Audition' looks like a talent tryout; its root sense is hearing. 'What a sight!' is said of something ugly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a place: a building site, a campsite, a spot on the map.

entries.clue: Whatever rhinoceros I name runs wild (4,4,2,5)

indicatorNotes.runs wild: letters running wild are scattered into a new order

annotation.surface: Whatever rhinoceros I give a name to goes on a rampage.
annotation.walkthrough: The rampaging rhino hides a 15-letter anagram; 'Whatever' works as the adverb 'no matter what'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom used as an adverb: 'I'll be there come rain or shine' means whatever happens.

entries.clue: Royal I back on one point (7)

blocks.note: the royal 'we' is a monarch's way of saying I
the stern is the back of a ship

annotation.surface: A monarch returns to make a point.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the point is a compass point, and the answer describes what lies toward it.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose definition: western describes what lies toward the west, one of the four compass points.

entries.clue: Shrink referring to Victorian book, struggle to cope (4,2,4,5)

blocks.note: to fall is to shrink or decrease
Hard Times is a Charles Dickens novel of 1854

annotation.surface: A psychiatrist discusses a Victorian novel and admits to struggling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' pretends to be slang for a psychiatrist; it is the verb meaning decrease.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: people who fall on hard times have lost money and struggle to cope.

entries.clue: Leader dismissed from awful party (4)

blocks.note: grave = dire, awful, as in a grave situation
the first letter, G, is removed

annotation.surface: A political leader sacked after a terrible party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leader' and 'party' suggest politics; the leader is just the first letter of the word for awful.
annotation.definitionFit: A modern sense: a rave is a large all-night dance party with electronic music.

entries.clue: Sovereign – item found in classroom? (5)

annotation.surface: A monarch visits a school.
annotation.walkthrough: A sovereign is also a British gold coin, a plausible false path; here it is the monarch.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a monarch who rules, and the straight measuring stick found on every school desk.

entries.clue: Mere in the middle, that is a lake (4)

indicatorNotes.in the middle: take the middle letters of the word

blocks.note: the middle two letters of mERe

annotation.surface: A mere, in the middle of the country, turns out to be a lake.
annotation.walkthrough: A mere is itself a lake, which tempts you to read 'Mere' as a definition; it only supplies its middle.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Erie is one of North America's five Great Lakes.

entries.clue: Australian native, well generous (5)

blocks.note: 'well!' and 'my!' are both exclamations of surprise

annotation.surface: Describing an Australian as a thoroughly generous person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Australian native' reads as a person; it is an animal. 'Well' is the interjection, not the adverb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of size: generous portions or rooms are ample, spacious.

entries.clue: Wine regularly opened by grandma, witless (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so take letters at a steady step, every second one
indicatorNotes.opened by: the outer letters are prised apart to hold another piece

blocks.note: nan is a British word for grandmother

annotation.surface: Grandma opens the wine and gets silly.
annotation.walkthrough: Grandma opening the wine is the picture; in the wordplay she sits between the wine's two alternate letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: inane remarks are empty and senseless.

entries.clue: Gate, hinge gone (7)

blocks.note: to hinge is to turn or pivot

annotation.surface: A gate whose hinge has vanished.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gate' sounds like a hinged door, which the hinge supports; in British sport the gate is the number of spectators.
annotation.definitionFit: A British sporting sense: the gate is the attendance at a match, which is how many people turned out.

entries.clue: Strain is back in part of joint (7)

indicatorNotes.back: read the word from the end
indicatorNotes.in: one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a tenon is the tongue of a mortise-and-tenon joint

annotation.surface: A strained back that sits in a joint.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as the body part that aches under strain; here it only turns a two-letter word round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: tension is the stress on a rope or a nerve.

entries.clue: Country pig overwhelmed by noises on farm (7)

blocks.note: ham is meat from a pig

annotation.surface: A country pig drowned out by the din of the farmyard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country' seems to describe the pig as rural; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Bahamas is an island nation in the Atlantic.

entries.clue: Live north of Urals after moving country (7)

indicatorNotes.north of: in a down entry the first piece sits above the second

blocks.note: to be is to live, exist

annotation.surface: Someone lives north of the Ural mountains after relocating.
annotation.walkthrough: The Urals are real Russian mountains, which makes the geography plausible; here they are just five letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Belarus is an Eastern European nation bordering Russia.

entries.clue: Parasite cleaner? (7)

blocks.note: a freeloader who lives off others
one who wipes things with a sponge

annotation.surface: A cleaner accused of being a freeloader.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the cleaning sense is an invented, literal one.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a freeloader who lives off others, and literally one who wipes with a sponge.

entries.clue: Miss school, rubbish on holiday (4,3)

annotation.surface: A pupil skips school, dismissing it as nonsense while on holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: This is British slang for playing truant.
annotation.definitionFit: British informal idiom: to bunk off is to play truant.

entries.clue: Old PM stripped of crowning glory, success (7)

blocks.note: a person's crowning glory is their hair

annotation.surface: A former prime minister loses his hair but wins anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: Stanley Baldwin was British Prime Minister three times between 1923 and 1937.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Stanley Baldwin led three British governments between 1923 and 1937.

entries.clue: Divine sources of silver etc. secured by payment (7)

blocks.note: silver and other metals are mined from ores

annotation.surface: Holy sources of silver, bought with a payment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Divine' looks like the adjective 'holy'; it is the verb, to predict, and 'sources of' tempts you toward first letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb sense of divine: to predict by insight, as a fortune-teller does.

entries.clue: Finn McCool, Fianna chap, champ ultimately (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: take the last letter of each word

blocks.note: the last letters of McCooL, FiannA, chaP, chamP

annotation.surface: Finn McCool, the champion warrior of the Fianna in Irish legend.
annotation.walkthrough: Finn McCool is an Irish mythical hero; the definition is just 'Finn', a person from the far north.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose geographical sense: Lapland spans northern Finland, so a Lapp may be a Finn.

entries.clue: Seriously upbeat (5)

blocks.note: British intensifier meaning very, as in 'good and proper'

annotation.surface: Being earnestly cheerful.
annotation.walkthrough: The two definitions seem opposed; in British usage the answer is also an intensifier meaning very, as in '___ good'.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the British intensifier (jolly good = very good) and the cheerful mood.

entries.clue: Nicked by students, a rotten old 11 Across (4)

indicatorNotes.Nicked by: stolen by the words that follow, so the answer is inside them

annotation.surface: A rotten old ruler gets arrested by students.
annotation.walkthrough: 11 Across is RULER, so the definition is 'old ruler'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: tsars were the emperors who ruled Russia until 1917.

entries.clue: Solid title provided that’s uplifting (4)

indicatorNotes.uplifting: in a down entry, lifting up reverses the letters

annotation.surface: A solid title, provided it's inspiring.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Uplifting' reads as inspiring; in a down clue it means read upward.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: firm ground and solid ground both hold steady underfoot.

entries.clue: Heading for shelter today, drifter? (4)

indicatorNotes.Heading for: take the head, the first letter

annotation.surface: A homeless drifter heads for a shelter today.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drifter' looks like a vagrant; with the question mark it is weather that forms drifts.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful definition: wind heaps snow into drifts, so it is a drifter.

entries.clue: Jazz Age passed in a riot, singer out of control (7,8)

annotation.surface: The Jazz Age went by in a wild whirl, with a singer out of control.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Passed' must first become a synonym before joining the anagram; only then do the fifteen letters add up.
annotation.definitionFit: A period name: the 1920s were called both the Jazz Age and the Roaring Twenties.

entries.clue: Boat, galley vessel? (7)

blocks.note: a galley is a ship's kitchen, and this vessel is a pan for steaming food

annotation.surface: A boat that is a galley ship.
annotation.walkthrough: A galley was an oared ship, so 'galley vessel' looks like a second boat; the galley is the kitchen and the vessel a cooking pot.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a steamship, and a cooking pot for steaming food in a ship's galley.

entries.clue: Failure of new hero, out of the running (7)

indicatorNotes.Failure of: the letters break down into a new order

annotation.surface: A new champion flops and loses the race.
annotation.walkthrough: In racing, a runner that 'came ___' finished unplaced.
annotation.definitionFit: A racing idiom: a horse that came nowhere finished unplaced, out of contention.
